Pancakes from around the world.Crêpe: Crêpes are thin French pancakes, and on Candlemas, February 2, tradition says to flip one while holding a coin to ensure a prosperous year.
Pancakes from around the world.Blini: Blini are small yeast-raised Russian pancakes, once linked to pagan sun rituals. They are served with caviar and sour cream, especially at Maslenitsa.
Pancakes from around the world.Okonomiyaki: Okonomiyaki is a Japanese savory pancake whose name means grilled as you like it. Osaka and Hiroshima make rival versions, and Hiroshima layers its ingredients.
Pancakes from around the world.Pajeon: Pajeon is a Korean scallion pancake, often eaten on rainy days with makgeolli rice wine. The sizzle of frying is said to sound like rain.
Pancakes from around the world.Dutch baby: The Dutch baby is a puffy oven-baked pancake invented in Seattle, not the Netherlands. The name is believed to come from a corruption of Deutsch.
Pancakes from around the world.Poffertjes: Poffertjes are fluffy Dutch mini pancakes made with yeast and buckwheat. They are cooked in a special dimpled pan and served with butter and powdered sugar.
Pancakes from around the world.Latke: Latkes are fried potato pancakes eaten at Hanukkah. The oil is the point, since it recalls the miracle of the temple lamp that burned for eight days.
Pancakes from around the world.Hotteok: Hotteok are Korean street pancakes filled with brown sugar, cinnamon, and nuts. They are a winter favorite, and the molten filling can burn a careless tongue.
Pancakes from around the world.Palatschinken: Palatschinken are thin Austrian and Hungarian pancakes, rolled with jam or sweet cheese. The word is believed to come from Latin placenta, meaning flat cake.
Pancakes from around the world.Pannekoek: The Dutch pannekoek is a large, thin pancake, often wider than a dinner plate. It can be savory with bacon or sweet with syrup.
Pancakes from around the world.Johnnycake: Johnnycakes are cornmeal pancakes from New England and the Caribbean. Rhode Island has long-running fights about how thick they ought to be.
Pancakes from around the world.Waffle: A waffle is cooked in a grid iron, not a pan, so it is a cake of a different kind. Belgian waffles became widely known in America at the 1964 World's Fair.
Pancakes from around the world.French toast: French toast is bread soaked in egg and fried, not a pancake. Its roots reach back to Roman times, and it is called pain perdu, lost bread, in France.
Pancakes from around the world.Tortilla: A tortilla is an unleavened flatbread, and in Spain a tortilla is an omelet of eggs and potato. Neither type is a pancake.
Pancakes from around the world.Naan: Naan is a leavened flatbread baked on the walls of a tandoor oven. It is bread, not a pan-fried pancake.
Pancakes from around the world.Pita: Pita puffs into a pocket in a very hot oven as steam inflates it. That makes it a bread, not a pancake.
Pancakes from around the world.Scone: A scone is a baked quick bread, not a pancake. A Scottish variant, the griddle scone, is cooked on a pan but is still a different thing.
Pancakes from around the world.English muffin: The English muffin was invented by an Englishman in New York in the 1880s, Samuel Bath Thomas. It is yeasted, griddled bread that is split before toasting.
Pancakes from around the world.Biscuit: An American biscuit is a flaky baked quick bread, quite unlike a pancake. The fat is cut into the flour, which makes it rise in layers.
Pancakes from around the world.Bagel: Bagels are boiled before being baked, which gives them their chewy crust. They are yeast bread, not pancakes.
Pancakes from around the world.Pretzel: Pretzels are dipped in lye, or baking soda, before baking, giving a dark, shiny crust. They are bread, not pancakes.
Pancakes from around the world.Strudel: Strudel is made of thin pastry dough wrapped around a filling and baked. The dough is stretched so thin that you should be able to read a newspaper through it.
Pancakes from around the world.Focaccia: Focaccia is an Italian oven-baked flatbread dimpled with olive oil. It resembles a pancake only in shape, and it is a yeast bread.
Pancakes from around the world.Brioche: Brioche is a rich French bread loaded with butter and eggs. It is baked in the oven, so it is not a pancake.

Whales and dolphins.Orca: Orcas, or killer whales, are actually the largest dolphins, and each pod has its own dialect of calls.
Whales and dolphins.Narwhal: The narwhal's 'horn' is a spiralled tusk, actually an elongated tooth that can reach about three metres in length.
Whales and dolphins.Beluga: Belugas are nicknamed 'canaries of the sea' for their whistles and clicks, and their white colour helps them blend in with Arctic ice.
Whales and dolphins.Humpback: Humpbacks sing complex songs that spread across oceans, and they blow bubble nets to trap fish.
Whales and dolphins.Blue whale: The blue whale is the largest animal ever known, with a heart roughly the size of a small car.
Whales and dolphins.Sperm whale: Sperm whales dive over a kilometre deep and have the largest brain of any animal, weighing about 8 kg.
Whales and dolphins.Porpoise: Porpoises are smaller and shyer than dolphins, with spade-shaped teeth and no beak, and the vaquita is the rarest marine mammal.
Whales and dolphins.Bottlenose: Bottlenose dolphins call each other with individual 'signature whistles' that work a bit like names.
Whales and dolphins.Minke: Minkes are the smallest baleen whales of the rorquals, and still can reach about nine metres long.
Whales and dolphins.Gray whale: Gray whales migrate up to around 20,000 km round trip, one of the longest journeys of any mammal.
Whales and dolphins.Pilot whale: Pilot whales are actually large dolphins, and they live in tight family pods that sometimes strand together.
Whales and dolphins.Bowhead: Bowhead whales may live over 200 years, and their enormous skulls can break through Arctic ice that's about a metre thick.
Whales and dolphins.Whale shark: Whale sharks are the largest fish, not whales; they're gentle filter feeders that belong with sharks.
Whales and dolphins.Manatee: Manatees are sirenians, not cetaceans; they graze on seagrass and are most closely related to elephants.
Whales and dolphins.Dugong: Dugongs are plant-eating sirenians, related to manatees and elephants rather than to whales and dolphins.
Whales and dolphins.Seal: Seals are pinnipeds, not cetaceans; they come ashore to breed, which whales and dolphins never do.
Whales and dolphins.Walrus: Walruses are pinnipeds, not whales, and their tusks can reach about a metre and help them haul out onto ice.
Whales and dolphins.Sea lion: Sea lions are eared seals that can walk on land using their flippers, which sets them apart from whales and dolphins.
Whales and dolphins.Otter: Sea otters rely on the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch, and they're not whales or dolphins.
Whales and dolphins.Basking shark: The basking shark is a huge filter-feeding fish, second only to the whale shark, yet it's a shark, not a whale.
Whales and dolphins.Mahi-mahi: Mahi-mahi is also called dolphinfish, but it's a fast-growing fish, unrelated to dolphins, which are mammals.
Whales and dolphins.Shark: Sharks are fish with gills; dolphins and whales are mammals that breathe air and nurse their young.
Whales and dolphins.Sea cow: 'Sea cow' is a nickname for manatees and dugongs, which are sirenians, not whales.
Whales and dolphins.Ichthyosaur: Ichthyosaurs looked just like dolphins but were marine reptiles, a classic example of convergent evolution; they went extinct long before whales.

Animals that would make terrible pets.Great white shark: It needs a huge ocean range, and attempts to keep one in an aquarium have usually failed within months.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Grizzly bear: Adults can weigh over 300 kilograms, and they eat enormous amounts of food, especially before winter.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Crocodile: A saltwater croc can live 70 years and has the strongest bite measured in any living animal.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Hippo: It looks placid, but the hippo is among Africa's deadliest large animals, and it can run about 30 kilometers an hour.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Box jellyfish: The box jellyfish carries venom among the deadliest on Earth, and its sting can stop a human heart within minutes.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Komodo dragon: The world's largest lizard can grow around 3 meters, has venom glands, and can take down a buffalo.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Rhino: A rhino can weigh over two tonnes, and its horn is made of keratin, the same stuff as fingernails.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Polar bear: It is the largest land carnivore, and its skin is black under its see-through fur.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Honey badger: Famously fearless, it will tackle venomous snakes and even lions, and it can escape from enclosures.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Cassowary: This Australian bird has a dagger-like claw about 12 centimeters long, and has been called the world's most dangerous bird.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Black mamba: One of the world's fastest snakes, it can move around 20 kilometers an hour, and its venom is deadly without antivenom.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Moose: The largest deer can weigh up to 700 kilograms and is surprisingly aggressive, especially when protecting calves.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Wolverine: A wolverine is a stocky weasel that can drive bears from their kills, and it ranges over huge territories.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Hamster: A hamster stores food in its stretchy cheek pouches, and it is nocturnal, so it's active when you sleep.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Goldfish: A well-kept goldfish can live over 20 years, far longer than most people expect.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Rabbit: Rabbits' teeth never stop growing, so they need constant chewing, and they can be litter-trained.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Guinea pig: They are social, so keeping a pair is recommended, and they cannot make their own vitamin C.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Budgie: Budgies can learn hundreds of words, and a few have been recorded with huge vocabularies.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Cat: Cats have been kept by people for about 10,000 years and purr at frequencies that may help heal bones.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Labrador: Labradors have been the most popular dog breed in the US for decades, and their coats are water-repellent.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Gerbil: Gerbils come from desert regions, so they drink little water, and they thump their feet when alarmed.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Canary: Miners once carried canaries underground as early warning for dangerous gas, and males sing the best.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Cockatiel: Cockatiels can mimic whistles and tunes, and their crest shows their mood.
Animals that would make terrible pets.Bearded dragon: This Australian lizard puffs out a spiny beard when threatened, and it is a popular, calm pet.

Salads.Caesar: Created in Tijuana in the 1920s by restaurateur Caesar Cardini, not by Julius Caesar. The original reportedly had no anchovies.
Salads.Waldorf: Created at New York's Waldorf Hotel in the 1890s from apples, celery and mayonnaise. Walnuts were added later.
Salads.Greek salad: Tomato, cucumber, olives and feta, typically with no lettuce. Called horiatiki in Greece, meaning village salad.
Salads.Niçoise: Salad from Nice with tuna, eggs, olives and anchovies. Purists insist that no cooked vegetables go in.
Salads.Caprese: Tomato, mozzarella and basil, echoing the Italian flag in color. It comes from the island of Capri.
Salads.Cobb: Created at the Brown Derby in Hollywood in the 1930s, reportedly from fridge leftovers. It has bacon, avocado, egg and blue cheese.
Salads.Tabbouleh: A Levantine herb salad built on finely chopped parsley with a little bulgur. Lebanon treats it as a national dish.
Salads.Fattoush: Levantine salad with fried or toasted pita pieces. Sumac gives it a tart lemony kick.
Salads.Panzanella: Tuscan salad of stale bread soaked with tomatoes. It was invented to use up old loaves.
Salads.Coleslaw: Shredded cabbage salad whose name comes from Dutch koolsla. It is a barbecue staple.
Salads.Som tam: Thai green papaya salad pounded in a mortar with chilies and lime. It comes from Laos and northeast Thailand.
Salads.Potato salad: Cold boiled potatoes in dressing. German style uses vinegar and bacon, while American uses mayonnaise.
Salads.Gazpacho: A cold soup rather than a salad. You drink or spoon it.
Salads.Hummus: A chickpea dip. You scoop it up, not toss it.
Salads.Guacamole: Mashed avocado dip. It is a dip, not a salad.
Salads.Tzatziki: Greek yogurt and cucumber dip. It is thick and creamy, a sauce more than a salad.
Salads.Bruschetta: Toasted bread topped with tomato and garlic. Its name comes from the Italian word for roasting over coals.
Salads.Ratatouille: Cooked vegetable stew. A salad would be raw.
Salads.Baba ganoush: Smoky mashed eggplant dip. Charred over a flame, it is a dip.
Salads.Spring roll: Wrapped fresh or fried. It is a roll, not a salad.
Salads.Tapenade: Provencal paste of olives, capers and anchovies. Its name comes from tapeno, meaning capers in Provencal.
Salads.Pesto: Sauce of basil, pine nuts, cheese and olive oil. It is named after pestare, to pound.
Salads.Minestrone: Hot Italian vegetable soup. A soup, not salad.
Salads.Borscht: Eastern European beet soup, served hot or cold. It is a soup.

Countries in North America.USA: The US includes Hawaii and Alaska, but Hawaii is in Oceania; geographically, Alaska's Denali is North America's highest peak.
Countries in North America.Canada: Canada has the longest coastline of any country, and more lakes than the rest of the world's countries combined, by most counts.
Countries in North America.Mexico: Mexico City sits on a drained lake bed that was once the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, and it's slowly sinking.
Countries in North America.Guatemala: Home to Tikal, a Maya city whose temples rise above the rainforest canopy, Guatemala is the most populous Central American country.
Countries in North America.Belize: Belize has the second-largest barrier reef in the world, and is the only Central American country with English as its official language.
Countries in North America.Honduras: Honduras holds the ruins of Copán, a major Maya city famed for its carved stone stairway of hieroglyphs.
Countries in North America.Cuba: The largest island in the Caribbean, Cuba is also home to the bee hummingbird, the smallest bird on Earth.
Countries in North America.Jamaica: Jamaica gave the world reggae, and Kingston's Bob Marley Museum sits in the singer's old home.
Countries in North America.Haiti: In 1804 Haiti became the first independent nation led by formerly enslaved people, after a successful revolution.
Countries in North America.Panama: The Panama Canal lets ships cross between the Atlantic and the Pacific without sailing around South America.
Countries in North America.Costa Rica: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948 and puts the savings into schools and nature; about a quarter of the land is protected.
Countries in North America.Bahamas: The Bahamas are an archipelago of about 700 islands, and the country lies in the Atlantic, not the Caribbean Sea.
Countries in North America.Nicaragua: Nicaragua has Lake Nicaragua, which holds freshwater sharks, and many volcanoes line its western side.
Countries in North America.Colombia: Colombia is in South America, the continent's northwest corner, and it's the only South American country with coasts on both the Caribbean and Pacific.
Countries in North America.Venezuela: Venezuela has Angel Falls, the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, at about 979 meters, in South America.
Countries in North America.Brazil: The largest country in South America, Brazil takes up nearly half the continent and is not part of North America.
Countries in North America.Ecuador: Ecuador is named for the equator, which crosses it just north of Quito, and it is in South America.
Countries in North America.Peru: Peru is in South America and home to Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel built high in the Andes.
Countries in North America.Guyana: Guyana is in South America, even though it is culturally closer to the Caribbean and plays cricket.
Countries in North America.Spain: Spain lies in Europe, though its Canary Islands sit off Africa, so no part of the country is in North America.
Countries in North America.Iceland: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, with part of it on the North American plate, but it's counted as Europe.
Countries in North America.Portugal: Portugal's Azores are in the mid-Atlantic and straddle the North American, Eurasian and African plates, but the country counts as Europe.
Countries in North America.Philippines: Spanish galleons shuttled between Manila and Acapulco for about 250 years, but the Philippines is in Asia, not North America.
Countries in North America.Chile: Chile is a long thin country in South America, up to about 4,300 km long and rarely wider than 200 km.

Not actually fish.Starfish: Sea stars are echinoderms, with no fins, gills or backbone. They can regrow a lost arm, and they have no brain.
Not actually fish.Jellyfish: Over 95 percent water, with no brain, bones or heart. Jellyfish have existed for roughly 500 million years, long before fish.
Not actually fish.Cuttlefish: A mollusc related to squid, not a fish. It can change color in a blink and has three hearts.
Not actually fish.Crayfish: A freshwater crustacean related to lobsters and crabs. It looks like a tiny lobster and is a staple of Louisiana cooking.
Not actually fish.Whale: A mammal, so it breathes air, nurses its calves and is warm-blooded. Whales descend from land animals related to hippos.
Not actually fish.Dolphin: A mammal that breathes air through a blowhole, and sleeps with half its brain at a time. Fish, by contrast, swish tails side to side.
Not actually fish.Octopus: A mollusc with three hearts and blue blood. It has about two thirds of its neurons in its arms.
Not actually fish.Sea cucumber: An echinoderm related to starfish, not a fish. Some can expel their own internal organs to deter predators, then regrow them.
Not actually fish.Lobster: A crustacean with a hard shell, not a fish. It can regrow lost claws, and its blood is clear until it hits the air.
Not actually fish.Squid: A mollusc with ten limbs, and no backbone. The colossal squid has the largest eyes of any animal.
Not actually fish.Shellfish: This catch-all for clams, shrimp and oysters isn't fish at all, since they lack backbones and fins.
Not actually fish.Seahorse: A trap: it's a real fish with gills and a backbone. It's the male that carries and gives birth to the young.
Not actually fish.Shark: A trap: a real fish, but its skeleton is made of cartilage, not bone. Some sharks lay eggs, and sharks have been around for 400 million years.
Not actually fish.Eel: A trap: it looks like a snake but is a real fish with gills. European eels travel thousands of kilometers to breed in the Sargasso Sea.
Not actually fish.Stingray: A trap: it is a true fish, a flat cousin of sharks with a cartilage skeleton, and it buries itself in sand to hide.
Not actually fish.Lungfish: A trap: it's a fish that can breathe air, and some species survive months in dried mud. It's still a true fish.
Not actually fish.Mudskipper: A trap: it's a fish that walks on mud using its fins and breathes through its skin. Still a fish.
Not actually fish.Clownfish: A trap: it's a real fish living among sea anemones. All start as male and some become female.
Not actually fish.Swordfish: A trap: a real fish, among the fastest in the ocean. Its sword is a flattened extension of the upper jaw.
Not actually fish.Moray: A trap: morays are fish, though they look like snakes. They have a second set of jaws in the throat.
Not actually fish.Pufferfish: A trap: it's a real fish that inflates by gulping water. Some species contain a deadly poison.
Not actually fish.Catfish: A trap: a real fish, with whisker-like barbels packed with taste buds. Some taste with their whole body.
Not actually fish.Flounder: A trap: a real fish that starts life with eyes on both sides, then one eye migrates to the other side.
Not actually fish.Tuna: A trap: a real fish, and unusually warm-blooded for a fish. Bluefin can cross whole oceans.

Subatomic particles.Proton: Positively charged, found in every atom's nucleus; the number of protons decides which element an atom is.
Subatomic particles.Neutron: Has no charge and sits in the nucleus; free neutrons decay in about 15 minutes, though inside atoms they can last forever.
Subatomic particles.Electron: Negatively charged and about 1,800 times lighter than a proton; the flow of them through wires is electricity.
Subatomic particles.Quark: Protons and neutrons are each made of three quarks; the name came from a line in James Joyce's Finnegans Wake.
Subatomic particles.Neutrino: Trillions pass through your body every second without a trace, as they almost never interact with matter.
Subatomic particles.Photon: A particle of light with no mass, and it carries the electromagnetic force; Einstein won his Nobel for showing light comes in these packets.
Subatomic particles.Muon: A heavier cousin of the electron; cosmic rays create them in the upper atmosphere, and they last only about two microseconds.
Subatomic particles.Positron: The antimatter twin of the electron; hospital PET scanners rely on positrons to image the body.
Subatomic particles.Gluon: The particle that glues quarks together inside protons; its name reflects exactly that job.
Subatomic particles.Higgs boson: Confirmed at CERN in 2012, it is tied to the field that gives other particles mass, and the press nicknamed it the God particle.
Subatomic particles.Tau: A very heavy, short-lived cousin of the electron, discovered in the 1970s; it lives for less than a trillionth of a second.
Subatomic particles.Atom: A trap: atoms are built from subatomic particles, so they are a level above. Despite the Greek name for uncuttable, they can be split.
Subatomic particles.Molecule: A trap: groups of atoms bonded together, so it is far bigger than a subatomic particle; water is a three-atom example.
Subatomic particles.Ion: A trap: an atom or molecule that lost or gained electrons; it is a charged atom, not a fundamental particle.
Subatomic particles.Isotope: A trap: a variant of an element with a different number of neutrons, so it is a kind of atom, not a particle.
Subatomic particles.Cell: A trap: the basic unit of life, made of trillions of atoms; your body holds roughly 30 trillion of them.
Subatomic particles.Virus: A trap: much larger than any subatomic particle, and often so small that thousands could fit across a hair's width.
Subatomic particles.Bacterium: A trap: a single-celled organism, unimaginably big compared to an electron, and more of them live in you than you'd guess.
Subatomic particles.Crystal: A trap: a crystal is a regular arrangement of countless atoms, so it is a structure and not a particle.
Subatomic particles.Compound: A trap: a substance made of different elements chemically bonded, such as salt, so it is far larger than a particle.
Subatomic particles.Polymer: A trap: a long chain of repeating molecules, like plastic or DNA, so it is enormous compared to subatomic particles.
Subatomic particles.Enzyme: A trap: a protein that speeds up chemical reactions in living things, so it is a big molecule, not a particle.
Subatomic particles.Dust mite: A trap: a microscopic animal about 0.3 mm long, which is millions of times bigger than any subatomic particle.
Subatomic particles.Grain of sand: A trap: a visible piece of rock, containing trillions of trillions of subatomic particles.

Things that can rust.Iron nail: Rust needs oxygen and water; the flaky oxide falls away and exposes fresh metal, so corrosion continues until the nail is gone.
Things that can rust.Steel wool: Its fine strands have huge surface area, so it can rust within hours when wet, and it will even burn if touched with a 9-volt battery.
Things that can rust.Cast iron pan: The baked-on oil called seasoning keeps moisture out, so a damp pan left on the rack is how most get rusty.
Things that can rust.Tin can: Mostly steel with a thin tin coating, so once scratched the steel underneath rusts.
Things that can rust.Wrought iron gate: It contains slag fibres that slow corrosion somewhat, yet gates still need paint to stay rust-free.
Things that can rust.Barbed wire: It is usually galvanised with zinc to delay rust, but when the coating wears away it corrodes.
Things that can rust.Bike chain: Steel links need oil, since a chain left out in rain can start rusting within days and then seize.
Things that can rust.Iron filings: Hand warmers work on this: iron powder rusts rapidly inside the pouch, and that oxidation releases heat.
Things that can rust.Steel girder: Rust takes up much more room than the iron it replaces, which is why it can burst concrete from inside.
Things that can rust.Horseshoe: Hung for luck, but an iron shoe left outdoors in damp conditions gets covered in rust.
Things that can rust.Iron railing: Rust expands as it forms, and it can crack the stone or concrete that holds a railing.
Things that can rust.Gold ring: Gold is so unreactive it does not corrode, so ancient gold artifacts still shine.
Things that can rust.Aluminum foil: It does not rust, as rust is specifically iron oxide; a thin aluminium oxide skin forms and shields the metal.
Things that can rust.Copper pipe: Copper turns green, not red-brown; the Statue of Liberty is green from the same copper patina.
Things that can rust.Plastic bottle: No iron to oxidise; plastics break down slowly under sunlight rather than rusting.
Things that can rust.Glass jar: Glass is essentially silicon dioxide, already oxidised, so it cannot rust.
Things that can rust.Silver spoon: Silver tarnishes black from sulfur compounds in air, which is a different reaction from rust.
Things that can rust.Titanium: Titanium forms an ultra-thin oxide film on contact with air, which is why it resists corrosion even in seawater and inside the body.
Things that can rust.Brass doorknob: A copper-zinc alloy with no iron, so it dulls but never rusts.
Things that can rust.Wooden fence: Wood rots or decays; rust only happens to iron-bearing metals.
Things that can rust.Bronze statue: Bronze grows a green patina, but with no iron it cannot rust.
Things that can rust.Platinum: It does not oxidise in air, which is partly why it is used for jewellery and catalytic converters.
Things that can rust.Rubber tire: A tire's rubber cracks from ozone and sunlight, but the steel belts hidden inside can rust if exposed.
Things that can rust.Diamond: Pure carbon can burn at around 800 degrees Celsius in oxygen, but it cannot rust.

Wes Anderson films.Rushmore: This 1998 film made Bill Murray and Jason Schwartzman stars. Schwartzman was a first-time actor when cast as the teen Max Fischer.
Wes Anderson films.The Royal Tenenbaums: This 2001 film of a gifted but dysfunctional family got an Oscar nomination for its script. It's set in a storybook New York.
Wes Anderson films.Moonrise Kingdom: Two kids run away on a fictional New England island in 1965. The 2012 film opened the Cannes Film Festival.
Wes Anderson films.Isle of Dogs: The 2018 film is shot in stop-motion with dogs exiled to a trash island in Japan. Anderson won Best Director at Berlin for it.
Wes Anderson films.Fantastic Mr. Fox: This 2009 stop-motion adaptation of Roald Dahl's book stars George Clooney. Voice actors recorded outdoors, not in studios.
Wes Anderson films.Asteroid City: A 2023 film set in a desert town in the 1950s, with a stage play inside the story. It mixes color and black-and-white.
Wes Anderson films.The French Dispatch: The 2021 film is a love letter to magazines like The New Yorker, told as a trio of stories in a fictional French town.
Wes Anderson films.Bottle Rocket: Anderson's 1996 debut began as a short film, and starred Owen and Luke Wilson. Owen co-wrote it with him.
Wes Anderson films.The Life Aquatic: Bill Murray plays an oceanographer in the 2004 film, much like Jacques Cousteau. Sound-wise, Seu Jorge sang David Bowie songs in Portuguese.
Wes Anderson films.Grand Budapest Hotel: The 2014 film won four Oscars and is set in a made-up Eastern European country. It was shot in Germany, in an old department store.
Wes Anderson films.Lady Bird: Greta Gerwig directed this 2017 coming-of-age film starring Saoirse Ronan. Not Anderson.
Wes Anderson films.Little Miss Sunshine: This 2006 road comedy was directed by Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris. Quirky like Anderson, but not his.
Wes Anderson films.Juno: Jason Reitman directed Juno (2007), and Diablo Cody won an Oscar for the script. Quirky, but not Anderson.
Wes Anderson films.Napoleon Dynamite: Jared Hess directed this 2004 cult comedy. It has a deadpan style that resembles Anderson's, but isn't his.
Wes Anderson films.Amelie: Jean-Pierre Jeunet directed this 2001 French film. Its whimsical look is Anderson-like, yet it isn't his.
Wes Anderson films.Her: Spike Jonze directed Her in 2013, a love story with an AI voiced by Scarlett Johansson. Not Anderson.
Wes Anderson films.Frances Ha: Noah Baumbach directed this 2012 black-and-white film. Baumbach co-wrote The Life Aquatic, but didn't direct it.
Wes Anderson films.Coraline: Henry Selick directed this 2009 stop-motion film. Anderson's stop-motion films are different ones.
Wes Anderson films.Paddington: Paul King directed Paddington (2014), whose dollhouse-style look reminds many of Anderson, but it's not his.
Wes Anderson films.Hugo: Martin Scorsese directed Hugo in 2011, a tribute to early filmmaker Georges Méliès. It was his first 3D film.
Wes Anderson films.Big Fish: Tim Burton directed Big Fish (2003). Its storybook feel resembles Anderson's, but he wasn't involved.
Wes Anderson films.Chef: Jon Favreau directed and starred in Chef (2014). It isn't an Anderson film.
Wes Anderson films.Nebraska: Alexander Payne directed this 2013 black-and-white film starring Bruce Dern. Not Anderson.
Wes Anderson films.Burn After Reading: The Coen brothers directed this 2008 spy comedy. Not Anderson, though both are known for oddball ensembles.

Spider-Man villains.Green Goblin: Norman Osborn, Peter Parker's friend's father, became the Goblin in the comics; Willem Dafoe played him in 2002.
Spider-Man villains.Doctor Octopus: Alfred Molina played the scientist with four mechanical arms in Spider-Man 2, often listed among the best superhero film villains.
Spider-Man villains.Venom: Venom is an alien symbiote that bonds with Eddie Brock, and it started as Spider-Man's black costume in the 1980s.
Spider-Man villains.Sandman: Flint Marko can become sand, and his comics origin is a physics accident on a beach.
Spider-Man villains.Vulture: Adrian Toomes, played by Michael Keaton in Spider-Man: Homecoming, uses a winged flight harness to steal technology.
Spider-Man villains.Electro: Max Dillon is an electrician who becomes a living power source; Jamie Foxx played him in 2014.
Spider-Man villains.Mysterio: Quentin Beck is a special-effects expert who fakes monsters, and Jake Gyllenhaal played him in Far From Home.
Spider-Man villains.Kraven: Kraven the Hunter, Sergei Kravinoff, stalks Spider-Man for sport and appears in comics since 1964.
Spider-Man villains.Lizard: Dr. Curt Connors tries to regrow his lost arm and turns into a reptilian monster.
Spider-Man villains.Rhino: A hulking thug in a powered suit with a horned helmet, Rhino is one of Spider-Man's longest-running enemies.
Spider-Man villains.Carnage: Cletus Kasady's symbiote is even more violent than Venom, which is his 'parent'.
Spider-Man villains.Scorpion: Mac Gargan, once a private investigator, was turned into a super-powered man with a tail.
Spider-Man villains.Shocker: Herman Schultz is a safecracker whose vibro-shock gauntlets send powerful blasts at Spider-Man.
Spider-Man villains.Joker: The Joker is Batman's archenemy, from DC, not Marvel's Spider-Man.
Spider-Man villains.Bane: Bane is the villain who broke Batman's back in DC comics, not Spider-Man's.
Spider-Man villains.Riddler: The Riddler is a Gotham villain, from DC, not a Spider-Man foe.
Spider-Man villains.Penguin: The Penguin is a Batman villain from DC, not Marvel.
Spider-Man villains.Magneto: Magneto is a Marvel villain, but he's a foe of the X-Men rather than Spider-Man.
Spider-Man villains.Thanos: Thanos is a Marvel villain, but he's an Avengers and Guardians foe, not Spider-Man's.
Spider-Man villains.Loki: Loki is Thor's brother, and Marvel's trickster, not typically Spider-Man's.
Spider-Man villains.Ultron: Ultron is the Avengers' robot foe, not a traditional Spider-Man villain.
Spider-Man villains.Red Skull: Red Skull is Captain America's nemesis, not Spider-Man's.
Spider-Man villains.Lex Luthor: Lex Luthor is Superman's DC archenemy, not Spider-Man's.
Spider-Man villains.Doctor Doom: Doctor Doom is the Fantastic Four's top villain, not Spider-Man's.

Famous cartoon cats.Garfield: Jim Davis launched Garfield in 1978, and Guinness lists it as the world's most widely syndicated comic strip.
Famous cartoon cats.Tom: Tom debuted in 1940 as 'Jasper' in Puss Gets the Boot, before William Hanna and Joseph Barbera renamed the pair Tom and Jerry.
Famous cartoon cats.Sylvester: Sylvester won an Oscar in 1957 for Birds Anonymous, a short in which he joins a support group to stop chasing birds.
Famous cartoon cats.Felix: Felix starred in the silent era, and in 1928 a Felix figurine reportedly served as an early TV test image because it held still.
Famous cartoon cats.Top Cat: Top Cat leads a gang of Manhattan alley cats; in Britain he was Boss Cat, because 'Top Cat' was already a cat food brand.
Famous cartoon cats.Scratchy: Scratchy, the black cat in The Simpsons' show-within-a-show, is mutilated endlessly by Itchy the mouse in gory slapstick.
Famous cartoon cats.Cheshire Cat: Lewis Carroll's cat can vanish piece by piece, leaving only a grin behind, which Alice calls a grin without a cat.
Famous cartoon cats.Figaro: Geppetto's tuxedo kitten in Pinocchio (1940) shares the workshop with Cleo the goldfish, whom he adores and annoys equally.
Famous cartoon cats.Puss in Boots: In the Shrek films, Antonio Banderas voices the swashbuckling cat, who earned his own spin-offs in 2011 and 2022.
Famous cartoon cats.Lucifer: Cinderella's smug, spoiled cat torments the mice Jaq and Gus, and his name is a pointed one: it is the devil's.
Famous cartoon cats.Duchess: The elegant white mother cat in The Aristocats, set in 1910 Paris, who has kittens Marie, Toulouse, and Berlioz.
Famous cartoon cats.Heathcliff: Created by George Gately, the orange street cat first appeared in a newspaper strip in 1973 before getting his own cartoons.
Famous cartoon cats.Marie: The white kitten of The Aristocats declares, 'Ladies do not start fights, but they can finish them!' and loves to paint.
Famous cartoon cats.Odie: A trap: Odie is a dog. The yellow, tongue-lolling pooch is Garfield's sidekick, and Garfield keeps kicking him off the table.
Famous cartoon cats.Snoopy: A dog, not a cat; NASA named the Apollo 10 lunar module Snoopy in 1969, and the command module Charlie Brown.
Famous cartoon cats.Pluto: A dog, not a cat; Mickey's pet debuted in 1930 as an unnamed bloodhound, the same year astronomers discovered the planet.
Famous cartoon cats.Scooby-Doo: A Great Dane, not a cat; the series premiered in 1969, and the name came from Frank Sinatra's scat singing in 'Strangers in the Night'.
Famous cartoon cats.Brian Griffin: The martini-drinking Family Guy dog is a dog, not a cat; he's a failed novelist who walks upright and talks like a person.
Famous cartoon cats.Droopy: A sad-faced dog, not a cat; Tex Avery created him in 1943, and he always catches villains while calmly greeting 'all you happy people'.
Famous cartoon cats.Spike: A bulldog, not a cat; in Tom and Jerry he is the grumpy dog who punishes Tom whenever the cat disturbs him or his son Tyke.
Famous cartoon cats.Jerry: Jerry is the mouse; in nearly every Tom and Jerry short, the tiny mouse outwits his cat enemy, despite being much smaller.
Famous cartoon cats.Tweety: Tweety is a canary, not a cat; he was drawn pink at first, then turned yellow after censors thought he looked naked.
Famous cartoon cats.Itchy: Itchy is the blue mouse in The Simpsons' cartoon-within-a-show; Scratchy is the cat, and Itchy attacks him endlessly.
Famous cartoon cats.Speedy Gonzales: A mouse, not a cat; this self-styled fastest mouse in Mexico often leaves Sylvester the cat in his dust.

Characters in Aladdin.Aladdin: The tale is not in the oldest Arabian Nights manuscripts. French translator Antoine Galland added it in the 1700s, and it is set in China.
Characters in Aladdin.Jasmine: Her name comes from the Persian word for the fragrant flower, and her rebellion against arranged marriage drives the film's plot.
Characters in Aladdin.Genie: Robin Williams improvised so heavily that animators had hours of recordings to sort through for the Genie's patter.
Characters in Aladdin.Jafar: Jafar shares his name with a real historical vizier, Ja'far al-Barmaki, who served the caliph Harun al-Rashid.
Characters in Aladdin.Iago: Real parrots mimic speech without understanding it, but Iago is a scheming parrot who keeps Jafar's plot moving with sarcasm.
Characters in Aladdin.Abu: Abu is a thief monkey whose name means 'father of' in Arabic, a common prefix in names across the Arab world.
Characters in Aladdin.Rajah: Rajah looks like a Bengal tiger, the most numerous tiger subspecies, and India holds most of the world's wild tigers.
Characters in Aladdin.The Sultan: The Sultan is Jasmine's toy-loving father, and Jafar's snake-headed staff briefly hypnotizes him into doing whatever he's told.
Characters in Aladdin.Magic Carpet: The Carpet has no face or voice, yet animators made it one of the film's most expressive characters with tassels, patterns and computer help.
Characters in Aladdin.Razoul: Razoul is the palace guard captain who chases Aladdin through the market in the opening 'One Jump Ahead' number.
Characters in Aladdin.Cave of Wonders: The Cave is a giant tiger head, and only a 'diamond in the rough' may enter. Touching the lamp's treasure triggers collapse.
Characters in Aladdin.Ali Baba: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves isn't in Aladdin, though both stories were added to Arabian Nights by Antoine Galland.
Characters in Aladdin.Sinbad: Sinbad the Sailor's seven voyages come from the Nights, and he starred in a 2003 DreamWorks film voiced by Brad Pitt.
Characters in Aladdin.Scheherazade: Scheherazade is the storyteller of the Nights who delays her execution by leaving each tale unfinished at dawn.
Characters in Aladdin.Mushu: Mushu comes from Mulan, not Aladdin. Eddie Murphy's fast-talking style echoes Robin Williams's Genie, which fooled some viewers.
Characters in Aladdin.Esmeralda: Esmeralda is the Romani dancer in Disney's The Hunchback of Notre Dame, based on Victor Hugo's 1831 novel.
Characters in Aladdin.Quasimodo: Hugo's bell ringer may be named after Quasimodo Sunday, the Sunday after Easter, when he was found as a baby.
Characters in Aladdin.Frollo: Judge Claude Frollo is Hunchback's villain, though in Hugo's novel he is an archdeacon, not a judge.
Characters in Aladdin.Hercules: Disney used the Roman name Hercules rather than the Greek Heracles, and Danny DeVito voiced his trainer Phil.
Characters in Aladdin.Megara: Meg is Disney's Hercules love interest, unusually cynical for a Disney heroine, and Susan Egan voiced her.
Characters in Aladdin.Pocahontas: The real Pocahontas, named Matoaka, was about ten when Jamestown was settled, so the film's romance with John Smith is invented.
Characters in Aladdin.John Smith: Captain John Smith led Jamestown, but Pocahontas was only around ten or eleven when they met, unlike in the film.
Characters in Aladdin.Meeko: Meeko belongs to Pocahontas, not Aladdin. A raccoon's front paws are so sensitive they feel objects better when wet.
Characters in Aladdin.Mowgli: Mowgli is the man-cub from Kipling's The Jungle Book, and Disney's 1967 film was Walt's last personally produced animated feature.

Things you'd yell during a game of tag.You're it: The classic line passes the role of chaser; the player who is 'it' is also called the tagger.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Not it: Called last to avoid being the first chaser; whoever is slowest to say it usually gets stuck.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Tag: Shouted with a touch; the game is also called 'tig' in Britain and 'it' in the US, and nearly every culture has a version.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Safe: Yelled on reaching home base or a protected spot, where you can't be tagged.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Can't catch me: A taunt associated with the Gingerbread Man, who was said to run as fast as he can.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Base: Yelled when touching a safe zone like a tree or wall.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.No tag backs: A rule stopping you from instantly tagging back whoever just tagged you.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Gotcha: A cry of triumph after a successful tag.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Freeze: Shouted to stop a chaser or in freeze tag, where a tagged player must stand still.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Checkmate: A chess line announcing the king is trapped; it comes from Persian 'shah mat', meaning the king is helpless.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Bingo: Yelled when completing a card; some claim it came from the game's old name 'beano'.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Uno: Called when you have one card left, and forgetting it costs two penalty cards.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Fore: A golfer's warning that a ball is flying toward others, probably a short form of 'before'.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Yahtzee: You yell it for five matching dice in one roll, which has odds of only about 1 in 1,296.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Touchdown: Football's scoring cry, worth six points, and a trap since it's not a tag call.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Timber: A lumberjack's warning that a tree is falling.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Strike: A bowling term for knocking down all ten pins in one roll, and a baseball call too.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Gin: A rummy card game, shouted when your hand is completely matched.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Marco: The call in Marco Polo, a pool game where the blindfolded player shouts it and others answer 'Polo'.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Goal: What you'd shout in soccer or hockey, not tag.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Jinx: Called when two people say the same thing at once, and the person who doesn't say it first must stay silent.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Rummy: A card game name, shouted to go out in some versions.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Snap: Yelled in the card game when two matching cards appear, and it's British.
Things you'd yell during a game of tag.Check: What you say when a chess king is threatened, not a tag call.

Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Park Lane: Park Lane is the second most expensive at 350 pounds, a real road along Hyde Park famed for luxury hotels.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Old Kent Road: Old Kent Road is the cheapest at 60 pounds. In London it is a long, ordinary road, the opposite of Mayfair.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Whitechapel Road: Whitechapel Road is the other 60-pound brown, in London's East End. It is the Monopoly twin of Old Kent Road.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Pall Mall: Pall Mall is a royal London street of gentlemen's clubs. Its name comes from a game, pall-mall, which resembles croquet.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Bond Street: Bond Street is a green property at 320 pounds, named after Sir Thomas Bond, a 17th-century developer.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Regent Street: Regent Street is one of the green set and a London shopping street designed by John Nash in the early 1800s.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Oxford Street: Oxford Street is a London shopping street famed for its crowds, and it's in the green set.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Piccadilly: Piccadilly is a yellow property, 280 pounds. The name comes from a type of lace collar sold nearby in the 17th century.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Strand: The Strand is in the red set at 220 pounds, a London street running between Westminster and the City.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Fleet Street: Fleet Street is red, 240 pounds, and was once the home of British newspapers, so the name still means the press.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Leicester Square: Leicester Square is yellow, 260 pounds, and is famed for its cinema premieres.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Boardwalk: Boardwalk is the US edition's top square, not the UK's. UK players pay for Mayfair instead.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Park Place: Park Place is Boardwalk's US partner. In the UK edition, the equivalent dark blue is Park Lane.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Baker Street: Baker Street is famous for Sherlock Holmes, but it is not on the board. The UK board has Marylebone station nearby.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Abbey Road: Abbey Road is famed for The Beatles' album cover, but it is not on the Monopoly board.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Downing Street: Downing Street is the home of the Prime Minister, but it's not on the board.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Carnaby Street: Carnaby Street is a famous 1960s fashion street in London, but it isn't on the board.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Portobello Road: Portobello Road is known for its antiques market, and not found on the Monopoly board.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Baltic Avenue: Baltic Avenue is part of the US game and has no British counterpart in the same position.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Marvin Gardens: Marvin Gardens is from the US board. The UK board's yellow set is Leicester Square, Coventry Street and Piccadilly.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Notting Hill: Notting Hill is a London district known for its carnival, but it's not on the board.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Covent Garden: Covent Garden is famous for its market and opera house, but it is not one of the UK board's squares.
Properties on the UK Monopoly board.Savile Row: Savile Row is famous for bespoke tailoring, but it is not on the board.

Mario Kart items.Star: The Star makes you invincible and fast for a few seconds and lets you bowl over opponents.
Mario Kart items.Lightning: Lightning shrinks every other racer and slows them, and it can also make them drop items.
Mario Kart items.Bob-omb: Bob-ombs are walking bombs that explode on impact or after a short time, and can be thrown ahead or behind.
Mario Kart items.Bullet Bill: Bullet Bill turns you into a missile that autopilots you along the track, invincible, and passes many racers.
Mario Kart items.Blooper: The Blooper squirts ink across rivals' screens so they can't see the road.
Mario Kart items.Super Horn: The Super Horn from Mario Kart 8 releases a shockwave that can destroy nearby items, even the blue shell.
Mario Kart items.Fire Flower: The Fire Flower lets you shoot fireballs that knock out rivals, and appears in a few of the series' entries.
Mario Kart items.Poke Ball: The Poke Ball is Pokemon's item, not in Mario Kart's item box.
Mario Kart items.Master Sword: The Master Sword is Link's legendary blade in The Legend of Zelda, though Link appears in Mario Kart 8 DLC.
Mario Kart items.Triforce: The Triforce is a sacred golden relic in Zelda made of three triangles: Power, Wisdom and Courage.
Mario Kart items.Chaos Emerald: Chaos Emeralds are the seven gems Sonic collects to turn into Super Sonic.
Mario Kart items.Power Pellet: The Power Pellet is the Pac-Man item that turns the ghosts blue so Pac-Man can eat them.
Mario Kart items.Energy Tank: The Energy Tank is a Metroid item that increases Samus's health capacity.
Mario Kart items.Rupee: Rupees are the Zelda currency, not a Mario Kart item.
Mario Kart items.Hookshot: The Hookshot is Link's grappling tool in Zelda.
Mario Kart items.Ocarina: The Ocarina is a Zelda instrument, central to Ocarina of Time, not a Kart item.
Mario Kart items.Pickaxe: The Pickaxe is a Minecraft tool, used to dig up ore.
Mario Kart items.Crowbar: The Crowbar is Half-Life's iconic weapon, carried by Gordon Freeman.
Mario Kart items.Portal gun: The Portal gun is the Aperture Science device from the Portal puzzle games and not a racing item.

Photography terms.Aperture: The adjustable lens opening is measured in f-numbers. The wider it is, the more light enters and the blurrier the background.
Photography terms.Shutter speed: How long the sensor sees light is it. A thousandth of a second freezes a hummingbird, and several seconds blurs a waterfall to silk.
Photography terms.ISO: The sensitivity setting is named after the international standards body, and raising it makes dim shots brighter but grainier.
Photography terms.Tripod: A three-legged stand holds a camera still for long exposures. Without one, night shots and low-light scenes come out smeared.
Photography terms.Exposure: This is the total amount of light that reaches the sensor. Aperture, shutter speed and ISO jointly set it, the exposure triangle.
Photography terms.Bokeh: From Japanese for blur, it describes how pleasingly a lens renders out-of-focus lights, like soft glowing discs behind a subject.
Photography terms.F-stop: Each full stop, such as f/2.8 to f/4, halves the light, and the odd numbers come from the area of the lens opening.
Photography terms.Viewfinder: The window photographers look through to frame a shot. Single-lens reflex cameras use a mirror to show exactly what the lens sees.
Photography terms.Lens cap: The humble cover protects glass from scratches, and it's among the most commonly lost camera accessories.
Photography terms.Flash: A burst of light lasting about a thousandth of a second lights up a dark subject, and its sudden burst causes red-eye.
Photography terms.Zoom lens: A lens that can change focal length without changing lenses, with a wide-to-telephoto range packed into a single barrel.
Photography terms.Macro: Close-up photography shows small subjects at life size or larger on the sensor, and true macro is at least 1:1 magnification.
Photography terms.Panorama: The word comes from Greek for all view, and it was coined by an Irish painter in 1787 for a huge circular painting.
Photography terms.Easel: A frame for holding a painter's canvas is an art tool. The word comes from the Dutch for donkey.
Photography terms.Palette: A painter's board for mixing colors is not photography, though the word is borrowed by digital image editing.
Photography terms.Kiln: This is a ceramic firing oven that can heat past 1,000 degrees Celsius, and it has nothing to do with film.
Photography terms.Glaze: A glassy coating on pottery that's fused by firing, it has nothing to do with taking pictures.
Photography terms.Purl: This knitting stitch is the mirror of the knit stitch and belongs to yarn crafts, not cameras.
Photography terms.Skein: A loosely coiled bundle of yarn, and the name is also used for a flock of geese. It's not a camera term.
Photography terms.Chisel: A woodworker's edged tool, used to carve or pare, it has no role in photography.
Photography terms.Lathe: This machine spins wood or metal against a blade, so it's a workshop tool and not a camera part.
Photography terms.Bobbin: A spool for thread, sitting inside a sewing machine, it's a sewing item, not a photography one.
Photography terms.Thimble: A sewer's fingertip cap is among the oldest tools of tailoring, and no part of any camera.
Photography terms.Gesso: An art-supply primer for canvas, made of chalk and glue, it belongs to painting rather than photography.

Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Waltz: Danced in three-four time, the waltz was once thought scandalous because partners held each other closely.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Tango: Born in the working-class ports of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, the tango is danced in a staccato, close hold with sharp head snaps.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Foxtrot: A smooth dance that was supposedly named after Harry Fox, a vaudeville performer, in 1914.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Quickstep: A lively dance from the 1920s combining the foxtrot with the Charleston, and with hops and skips that must look light.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Viennese waltz: Fast, at about 58 bars a minute, with continuous turns; it is the oldest of the standard ballroom dances.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Cha-cha: A Cuban dance whose name imitates the sound of dancers' shuffling feet in its triple step.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Rumba: Called the dance of love, this slow Cuban dance emphasises hip movement, and is the base of the Latin-dance family.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Samba: Brazil's carnival dance, known for a bouncing hip action, and which was adapted for ballroom competition.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Paso doble: A dance based on a bullfight, where the man plays the matador and the woman his cape, and it's Spanish in style.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Jive: A fast, bouncy Latin dance and the competition version of swing, taking its flicks and kicks from American jitterbug.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Breakdance: A street dance developed in the Bronx in the 1970s, made a medal event at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Hip hop: A street style that grew with the music from the Bronx, and not a ballroom competitive dance.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Tap: Sound is made by metal plates on the shoes, and the style grew out of Irish step and African rhythms.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Ballet: A formal stage art from the Italian and French courts, and not a ballroom event.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Moonwalk: A glide-backward trick made famous by Michael Jackson in 1983, but not a dance style.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Macarena: A 1990s party dance of choreographed arm moves, which topped charts in 1996.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Floss: A hip-swinging dance craze of the late 2010s, popularised by a Fortnite emote and a kid called Backpack Kid.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Haka: A Maori war dance and chant, most famously performed by New Zealand's rugby team, the All Blacks.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Conga: A Cuban line dance, whose name comes from the drum, and it is a party dance, not a competitive ballroom one.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Hokey pokey: A children's party song and dance with 'put your left foot in', called the hokey cokey in Britain.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Robot: A popping-style dance mimicking mechanical movement, part of street dance and not ballroom.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Can-can: A high-kicking cabaret dance from 19th-century Paris, and once banned as scandalous.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Limbo: A party game that began in Trinidad, in which dancers bend backwards under a lowered bar.
Competitive ballroom and Latin dances.Clogging: An Appalachian folk dance with stomping footwork, not a ballroom competition dance.

Things on a golf course.Fairway: The closely mown strip between tee and green, and its name came from the open sea lane through which ships travelled.
Things on a golf course.Green: The finely cut grass around the hole, mowed to a few millimetres, and putts on it roll fast and show subtle slopes.
Things on a golf course.Bunker: A sand trap, and the word comes from Scots for a chest or bench, and the original ones were hollows in coastal dunes.
Things on a golf course.Rough: Longer grass along the fairway that penalizes wayward shots, and it can be thick enough to swallow a ball.
Things on a golf course.Tee box: The starting area for each hole, with markers showing the distance for different players, and tees were once piles of sand.
Things on a golf course.Water hazard: A pond, creek or lake, and a ball that lands in it costs a penalty stroke, a feature famously dominant on the 17th at TPC Sawgrass.
Things on a golf course.Flagstick: The pole in the hole, which players can leave in or take out for putts, and the rules now allow either.
Things on a golf course.Clubhouse: The social and administrative centre of a golf course, and the 19th hole is the golfers' nickname for its bar.
Things on a golf course.Dogleg: A hole that bends like a dog's hind leg, and golfers have to decide whether to cut the corner.
Things on a golf course.Pin: Another word for the flagstick, and a hole location for the day is called the pin position.
Things on a golf course.Cup: A hole is 4.25 inches wide, a size reportedly chosen from a common pipe used by an early Scottish greenkeeper.
Things on a golf course.Driving range: A place to hit balls without playing a course, and it's the best way to practise a swing.
Things on a golf course.Fringe: The short collar of grass around the green, and a ball resting on it can often be putted.
Things on a golf course.Dugout: A shelter for baseball players at the side of the field, and no golf course has one.
Things on a golf course.Pitcher's mound: A raised patch of dirt for the baseball pitcher, 10 inches higher than home plate, and there's no such mound in golf.
Things on a golf course.End zone: The scoring area at either end of an American football field, and golf has no end zones.
Things on a golf course.Crease: The area in front of a hockey or lacrosse goal, and also a cricket batting line, but it's not golf.
Things on a golf course.Penalty spot: A soccer mark 12 yards from goal, and golf has no such thing.
Things on a golf course.Baseline: A tennis or basketball boundary, and a baseball path between bases, and it's not part of golf.
Things on a golf course.Oche: The line from which darts players throw, a British pub word of uncertain origin, and nothing to do with golf.
Things on a golf course.Hog line: A line on curling ice that a stone must cross to remain in play, and it's absent on a golf course.
Things on a golf course.Blue line: An ice hockey line that defines the attacking zone, and not a golf feature.
Things on a golf course.Free-throw line: A basketball line 15 feet from the hoop, and not found on the fairway.
Things on a golf course.Halfway line: A soccer line dividing the pitch into two equal halves, and no such line exists on a golf course.

Gods of the sea.Poseidon: The Greek sea god, whose trident was said to cause earthquakes. He lost a contest to Athena for Athens.
Gods of the sea.Neptune: The Roman sea god and the eighth planet's namesake. It was found in 1846 by calculation before anyone saw it.
Gods of the sea.Njord: The Norse sea and wind god, who kept ships and fishers safe. He married the giantess Skadi, but they couldn't agree on where to live.
Gods of the sea.Aegir: The Norse sea giant who hosted feasts for the gods, brewing ale in a huge cauldron. His wife Ran dragged sailors down with a net.
Gods of the sea.Oceanus: A Titan who personified the great river circling the world. The word "ocean" comes from him.
Gods of the sea.Nereus: The "old man of the sea," a kindly sea god and father of fifty Nereids. He could change shape like Proteus.
Gods of the sea.Proteus: A shape-shifting sea god who herded Poseidon's seals. Our word "protean," meaning changeable, comes from him.
Gods of the sea.Triton: Poseidon's son, a merman who calmed or stirred waves by blowing a conch shell. Neptune's largest moon is named after him.
Gods of the sea.Tangaroa: The Polynesian and Maori god of the sea. In some stories, the sea is his body.
Gods of the sea.Manannan: An Irish and Manx sea god who cloaked the Isle of Man in mist. He's the island's legendary protector.
Gods of the sea.Pontus: The Greek primordial god of the sea. He's older than Poseidon and son of Gaia.
Gods of the sea.Zeus: King of the sky and thunder in Greek myth. The sea belonged to his brother Poseidon.
Gods of the sea.Ares: The Greek war god, with no connection to the sea.
Gods of the sea.Thor: The Norse thunder god, who fights giants. He did fish for the world serpent, but he isn't the sea's god.
Gods of the sea.Ra: The Egyptian sun god, sailing the sky in a boat. Not a sea god.
Gods of the sea.Apollo: A Greek god of sun, music and prophecy, with no sea domain.
Gods of the sea.Odin: Norse chief god of wisdom, war and poetry.
Gods of the sea.Hades: Greek god of the underworld. His realm is under the earth, not the sea.
Gods of the sea.Hermes: The Greek messenger and god of travelers and trade. Not a sea god.
Gods of the sea.Mars: The Roman war god and the red planet's namesake. Not tied to the sea.
Gods of the sea.Vulcan: The Roman god of fire and forges. He works with fire, not water.
Gods of the sea.Anubis: The Egyptian jackal-headed god of the dead, not of the sea.
Gods of the sea.Athena: Greek goddess of wisdom and war. She did win Athens from Poseidon with an olive tree, but she isn't a sea deity.
Gods of the sea.Demeter: Greek goddess of the harvest and farming, not the sea.

Gods and goddesses of war.Ares: The Greek god of brutal, bloodthirsty war, whom even Zeus called the most hateful of gods. Athena, who fights with strategy, usually beat him.
Gods and goddesses of war.Mars: Roman war god, more respected than Ares, and father of Romulus and Remus. The month March and the red planet are named for him.
Gods and goddesses of war.Tyr: The Norse god of war and justice, who lost his hand placing it in Fenrir's jaws as a pledge. Tuesday is named after him.
Gods and goddesses of war.Athena: Greek goddess of wise warfare and strategy, born fully armored from Zeus's head. The Parthenon was built in her honor.
Gods and goddesses of war.Bellona: The Roman war goddess, sister or wife of Mars. Her temple stood outside Rome's sacred boundary, where the Senate received foreign envoys.
Gods and goddesses of war.Sekhmet: The lioness-headed Egyptian goddess of war and plague. Myth says Ra tricked her with beer dyed red to stop her slaughter.
Gods and goddesses of war.Montu: A falcon-headed Egyptian war god of Thebes, favored by warrior pharaohs. His name is often seen in the royal names Mentuhotep.
Gods and goddesses of war.Enyo: A Greek goddess of bloodshed and destruction who accompanied Ares into battle. She is also linked to the sacking of cities.
Gods and goddesses of war.Huitzilopochtli: The Aztec war and sun god, whose name means "hummingbird of the south." The Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan was dedicated to him.
Gods and goddesses of war.Aphrodite: Greek goddess of love. She did have an affair with Ares, but she's no war goddess.
Gods and goddesses of war.Venus: The Roman goddess of love and beauty. She is Mars's famous lover, not a goddess of war.
Gods and goddesses of war.Hestia: The goddess of the hearth, calm and peaceful, who swore to stay virgin forever. Nothing to do with war.
Gods and goddesses of war.Demeter: Greek goddess of grain. She is nurturing, not warlike.
Gods and goddesses of war.Ceres: Roman goddess of agriculture, whose name gives us "cereal." Not a war deity.
Gods and goddesses of war.Dionysus: Greek god of wine and revelry. His following was wild, but his domain wasn't war.
Gods and goddesses of war.Bacchus: The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstasy.
Gods and goddesses of war.Hermes: The Greek messenger, thieves' and travelers' god. Not a war god, though he sometimes guided armies.
Gods and goddesses of war.Frigg: The Norse queen of the gods and goddess of marriage and foresight. Friday comes from her name.
Gods and goddesses of war.Bastet: The Egyptian cat goddess of home and protection. In early times she was lion-headed and more warlike, but later she was gentle.
Gods and goddesses of war.Vesta: The Roman goddess of the hearth, whose sacred flame was tended by the Vestal Virgins. She is a goddess of home.
Gods and goddesses of war.Iris: The Greek goddess of the rainbow and the gods' messenger.
Gods and goddesses of war.Hypnos: The Greek god of sleep, twin of Thanatos, who is death. The word "hypnosis" comes from him.
Gods and goddesses of war.Eros: Greek god of love, not war, though he is the son of Ares and Aphrodite in some versions.
Gods and goddesses of war.Baldur: The Norse god of light and beauty, whom nothing could harm except mistletoe. His death by Loki's trick was seen as the start of Ragnarok.

Scientists born before 1600.Galileo: Italian astronomer, born 1564, who used a telescope to find Jupiter's four big moons. He was tried by the Inquisition in 1633.
Scientists born before 1600.Copernicus: Born in 1473, he proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun. His book was published in 1543, the year he died.
Scientists born before 1600.Kepler: Born 1571, he worked out that planets orbit in ellipses, not circles. He used Tycho's data to do it.
Scientists born before 1600.Archimedes: Greek of Syracuse, born about 287 BC. He found the principle of buoyancy, and the legend says he shouted 'Eureka' in the bath.
Scientists born before 1600.Euclid: Greek mathematician of about 300 BC. His Elements was a standard geometry textbook for over two thousand years.
Scientists born before 1600.Ptolemy: Born around AD 100, he wrote the Almagest, placing Earth at the centre of the universe, an idea that lasted over 1,400 years.
Scientists born before 1600.Tycho Brahe: Danish astronomer born 1546, who lost part of his nose in a duel and wore a metal replacement. His precise observations made Kepler's laws possible.
Scientists born before 1600.Hippocrates: Ancient Greek physician born about 460 BC, the 'father of medicine', whose name lives in the doctors' oath.
Scientists born before 1600.Aristotle: Born 384 BC, he was Alexander the Great's tutor, and wrote on biology and physics. His ideas dominated science for centuries.
Scientists born before 1600.Avicenna: Born 980, the Persian author of the Canon of Medicine, used in European universities until the 1600s.
Scientists born before 1600.William Harvey: Born 1578, English physician who first described blood circulating around the body, pumped by the heart.
Scientists born before 1600.Vesalius: Born 1514, the Flemish anatomist whose 1543 book on the human body corrected errors of ancient authorities by actually dissecting.
Scientists born before 1600.Isaac Newton: Trap: born in 1642, after 1600. His laws of motion and gravity came decades later than the others here.
Scientists born before 1600.Charles Darwin: Trap: born in 1809, he proposed evolution by natural selection, about two centuries after 1600.
Scientists born before 1600.Marie Curie: Trap: born in 1867, she won two Nobel Prizes, in physics and chemistry, in the 20th century.
Scientists born before 1600.Tesla: Trap: born in 1856, an electrical engineer who worked on AC power, far later than 1600.
Scientists born before 1600.Michael Faraday: Trap: born in 1791, he discovered electromagnetic induction, a nineteenth-century scientist.
Scientists born before 1600.Gregor Mendel: Trap: born in 1822, the monk whose pea plant experiments founded genetics, a 19th-century figure.
Scientists born before 1600.Niels Bohr: Trap: born in 1885, the Danish physicist who modelled the atom, so a 20th-century scientist.
Scientists born before 1600.Lavoisier: Trap: born in 1743, the French chemist who named oxygen and helped found modern chemistry. After 1600.
Scientists born before 1600.Benjamin Franklin: Trap: born in 1706, the American statesman who studied lightning. He's well after 1600.
Scientists born before 1600.Carl Linnaeus: Trap: born in 1707, the Swedish naturalist who devised the system for naming species. Well after 1600.
Scientists born before 1600.Einstein: Trap: born in 1879, long after 1600, and best known for relativity, so not an early scientist.
Scientists born before 1600.Louis Pasteur: Trap: born in 1822, the French microbiologist who developed vaccines and pasteurization, much later than 1600.

Things that come in a can.Soup: Canned soup made Campbell's famous, and in 1962 Andy Warhol painted 32 canvases of its soup cans.
Things that come in a can.Paint: Paint cans have a rim channel so the lid seals tight, which is why you pry it open with a screwdriver.
Things that come in a can.Soda: The soda can's pull tab was invented in 1959 by Ermal Fraze, and it was replaced by the stay-on tab in the 1970s.
Things that come in a can.Tuna: Canned tuna became a staple after 1900s California canners found albacore turned pale like chicken, hence the nickname.
Things that come in a can.Baked beans: Heinz baked beans were first sold in the UK in 1901, and the British now eat more of them than anyone else.
Things that come in a can.Hairspray: Hairspray goes in an aerosol can, a format whose spray was developed from bug-killing propellants used in World War II.
Things that come in a can.Whipped cream: Whipped cream cans use nitrous oxide, which dissolves into the fat and expands as the cream squirts out.
Things that come in a can.Chopped tomatoes: Canned tomatoes are often fresher than store tomatoes because they are packed within hours of picking.
Things that come in a can.Spray paint: Spray paint cans have a small steel ball inside that rattles, which mixes the pigment as you shake it.
Things that come in a can.Sweetcorn: Sweetcorn is canned in brine or water, a process invented in the early 1800s and taken up for soldiers.
Things that come in a can.Shaving foam: Shaving foam leaves the can as a liquid gel and puffs into foam as the propellant gas expands, ready to soften whiskers.
Things that come in a can.Dog food: Canned dog food debuted in 1922, when Chappel Brothers began selling a horse meat product called Ken-L-Ration.
Things that come in a can.Bread: Bread is sold in bags or loaves, though a famous Boston brown bread is actually steamed in a can.
Things that come in a can.Eggs: Eggs ride in cartons because their shells are fragile, and the egg carton itself dates from 1911.
Things that come in a can.Bananas: Bananas have their own wrapper, the peel, and they are the world's most traded fresh fruit.
Things that come in a can.Cereal: Cereal is sold in a cardboard box with a plastic liner, and puffed grains are fluffed with steam pressure.
Things that come in a can.Toothpaste: Toothpaste comes in a tube, a format borrowed from artists' paint in the 1890s.
Things that come in a can.Crayons: Crayons are sold in cardboard boxes, and their wax is made from paraffin.
Things that come in a can.Spaghetti: Spaghetti in a can does exist, but dry spaghetti is sold in boxes or bags, sometimes in a tall pack.
Things that come in a can.Yogurt: Yogurt usually comes in a cup or tub, because the live cultures need a lightly sealed container.
Things that come in a can.Lettuce: Lettuce is sold fresh as a head or in a bag; it is almost never canned because the leaves go limp.
Things that come in a can.Ice cream: Ice cream comes in a tub or carton, because cans would shut out the air that makes it scoopable.
Things that come in a can.Sliced cheese: Sliced cheese comes in a plastic pack, and the individually wrapped kind is a processed cheese food.
Things that come in a can.Cotton swabs: Cotton swabs were invented in the 1920s and sold in a small box or tub, never a can.

Things that beep.Microwave: Its beep signals the end of cooking, and beeps are used because they carry well and are easy to hear from another room.
Things that beep.Smoke detector: The low-battery chirp often starts at 3 am because cooler nighttime air makes a weak battery drop below the threshold.
Things that beep.Alarm clock: Early alarm clocks used bells, and electronic beeping came with digital clocks in the 1970s.
Things that beep.Barcode scanner: The first product scanned was a pack of Wrigley's gum in 1974, in a store in Ohio.
Things that beep.Reversing truck: Trucks use beepers by law in many countries, and 'white noise' alarms are an alternative that are easier to locate.
Things that beep.Heart monitor: The beep follows each heartbeat, and a flat continuous tone signals no detectable heart activity.
Things that beep.Kitchen timer: The first kitchen timer was patented in the 1920s, and many were shaped like tomatoes or eggs.
Things that beep.Metal detector: Detectors beep when metal disturbs a magnetic field, which can reveal anything from coins to ancient hoards.
Things that beep.Pager: Pagers beeped to say someone was calling, and some hospitals still use them since their signal reaches indoors.
Things that beep.Parking sensor: Ultrasonic sensors measure distance using echoes, much like a bat, and beep faster as you approach.
Things that beep.Cuckoo clock: It doesn't beep: the cuckoo call comes from small bellows pushing air through two tiny pipes.
Things that beep.Wind chime: Chimes ring rather than beep, and different tube lengths produce different notes.
Things that beep.Church bell: Bells are cast bronze, and large ones are tuned by shaving metal from inside.
Things that beep.Whistling kettle: It whistles, not beeps, because steam rushes through a small opening and vibrates.
Things that beep.Rubber duck: A squeaky duck squeaks as air is forced through a small reed or hole, not a beeping electronic sound.
Things that beep.Harmonica: A harmonica makes tones from vibrating reeds, and a single instrument can be small enough to fit in a pocket.
Things that beep.Rain stick: The sound of falling rain is made by pebbles or seeds falling past cactus spines or pins inside the tube.
Things that beep.Maraca: Maracas rattle with seeds or beads inside a gourd, and are a staple of Latin music.
Things that beep.Bicycle bell: A bike bell dings, rather than beeps, because a small striker hits a metal dome.
Things that beep.Pillow: A pillow is silent, which is its entire virtue.
Things that beep.Candle: Candles are silent, burning with a flame that is hot at the center and quiet.
Things that beep.Broom: A broom swishes rather than beeps, and its bristles were once made from broom plants, hence the name.
Things that beep.Teapot: Teapots are quiet; if you hear a beep, it's the kettle's cousin or a timer.
Things that beep.Grandfather clock: A grandfather clock chimes or strikes, and the tall case houses the long pendulum.

Things on a front door.Doorknob: The doorknob as we know it was patented in the 1800s, and the word 'knob' goes back centuries; many are still made of brass.
Things on a front door.Mail slot: Letter slots in doors only spread in the 1800s, after postal services began delivering to each house rather than a central place.
Things on a front door.Peephole: A peephole uses a wide-angle fisheye lens, which lets you see a broad view outside, but the view only works in one direction.
Things on a front door.Door knocker: Door knockers in the shape of lions or hands, like the hand of Fatima, were believed to ward off evil and welcome good luck.
Things on a front door.Door chain: A door chain lets the door open a few inches, but it is easily broken by force, so it's more for peace of mind than real security.
Things on a front door.Keyhole: Keyholes are often decorative as much as functional, and the old 'skeleton key' style could open many different locks.
Things on a front door.Hinges: Hinges are among the oldest hardware: ancient Egyptians used simple pivots, and the pins in a hinge are usually removable on the inside.
Things on a front door.Deadbolt: A deadbolt can't be pushed back with a credit card, unlike a spring latch, which is why it's the strongest lock on most doors.
Things on a front door.Kick plate: A kick plate is a metal panel on the lower part of a door that protects it from scuffs from shoes and from cleaning supplies.
Things on a front door.Window box: A window box hangs on the window's ledge, not the door; it's often planted with trailing flowers like petunias or geraniums.
Things on a front door.Chimney: A chimney sits high on the roof, and in the days before safety, boys were sent to climb inside to clean them.
Things on a front door.Gutter: The gutter runs along the roof edge, and a typical one carries thousands of gallons of rainwater in a year.
Things on a front door.Doormat: The doormat sits in front of the door, not on it; it gets the muddy footprints so the floors inside don't.
Things on a front door.Porch light: The porch light usually hangs beside the door or above it, so it's near the door but not actually on it.
Things on a front door.Garden gate: The garden gate is at the edge of the property, not the house, so it never ends up on the front door.
Things on a front door.Garden gnome: Garden gnomes were first made in 1800s Germany, and they stand in the garden rather than on any door.
Things on a front door.Drainpipe: A drainpipe runs down the wall, and its job is to carry rainwater from roof gutters safely to the ground.
Things on a front door.Satellite dish: A satellite dish is usually fixed to the wall or roof, and it must point at a satellite roughly 22,000 miles up.
Things on a front door.Roof tile: Roof tiles go up high on the roof; clay ones can last a century or more if they're looked after.
Things on a front door.Window shutters: Shutters flank windows, and they began as a protection against weather and later became a style feature.
Things on a front door.Weather vane: A weather vane points into the wind, so it's mounted on the very top of a roof, far from the front door.
Things on a front door.TV aerial: A TV aerial is on the roof or an upper wall, as high as possible to catch the broadcast signal.
Things on a front door.Flower bed: The flower bed is in the ground by the house; the classic English cottage garden mixes dozens of plants in one bed.
Things on a front door.Driveway: A driveway leads up to the house; the word was first used in the 1800s for a drive that went to a house.

Ways to pay for something.Cash: Cash is the oldest way to pay still in use, though some countries like Sweden now see very little of it.
Ways to pay for something.Credit card: Credit cards let you borrow for a purchase and settle later, and Diners Club issued the first general-purpose one in 1950.
Ways to pay for something.Debit card: A debit card pulls money directly from your bank account, so you can't spend what you don't have.
Ways to pay for something.Check: Checks date back centuries; goldsmiths and merchants used bills of exchange as early as medieval times.
Ways to pay for something.Gift card: Gift cards are essentially prepaid money, and billions of dollars on them go unspent each year.
Ways to pay for something.Smartphone: Phones pay through NFC chips, and a tap uses a one-time code so your real card number stays hidden.
Ways to pay for something.Smartwatch: A smartwatch can pay with a tap at a terminal, so you don't even need to pull your wallet out.
Ways to pay for something.Coins: Coins are among the oldest money, with the first ones minted in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 600 BC.
Ways to pay for something.Bank transfer: A bank transfer moves money directly between accounts, and is the usual way to pay rent or large bills.
